solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Monocle, say, decking the outdated girl

indicators.note: to deck is to adorn or wrap round, so the abbreviation for 'say' is wrapped round the old word

parts.note: EG, for example, is the abbreviation signalled by 'say'
YE is the archaic spelling of the definite article, as in 'Ye Olde Shoppe'
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned girl dressed up with a monocle, it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monocle, say' looks like a definition by example, but 'say' gives EG and the monocle stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A monocle is a single corrective lens worn in one eye, a type of eyeglass.

clue.text: Eulogy, off and on, uplifted solver?

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted up means the letters are read from bottom to top
taking letters on and off picks every other one of the word

parts.note: every other letter, starting with the second, of this word

explanation.surface: A solver cheered by a glowing tribute now and again.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords often address the solver directly, so the definition is the second-person pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: From the setter's side of the page the solver is the person spoken to, addressed as the pronoun.

clue.text: Is broadcast guest drunk when hosting Oscars now and then?

indicators.note: a drunk word is a reeling, rearranged one, here applied to the whole group
the guest word hosts the extra letters, so all go into the mix together

parts.note: taken as written
Oscar is O in the radio alphabet; two Oscars at different moments give two O's

explanation.surface: A drunken guest at the Academy Awards ceremony goes out on air.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar is O in the radio alphabet, and 'now and then' signals two separate occasions, two O's, which mix in with the guest's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme that goes out is transmitted, the same idea as being broadcast.

clue.text: Genuine gold article linked to endless lure

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
'the' is the definite article

indicators.note: with no ends, so the first and last letters of the word are both dropped

parts.note: to lure is to entice

explanation.surface: Real gold bait for an angler, as a piece of jewellery advertising might put it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' here strips both ends, not just the tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Something authentic is real, not counterfeit, which is what genuine means.

clue.text: In hospital, encountered ace composer

indicators.note: one piece goes in the other, here the verb inside the hospital word

parts.note: a san, short for sanatorium, is a hospital
met means encountered
A is the ace in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: Someone in hospital met a brilliant composer there.
explanation.walkthrough: Bedrich Smetana was the Czech composer of 'Ma Vlast' and 'The Bartered Bride'.
explanation.definitionFit: Smetana was a nineteenth-century Czech musician who wrote operas and symphonic poems.

clue.text: Nonsense surrounds development of epic muscles

indicators.note: the nonsense word goes round the other piece

parts.note: BS is a slang abbreviation for nonsense

indicators.note: a development is a working-out into new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Talk of bodybuilders developing epic muscles is dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Biceps are the large flexor muscles at the front of the upper arm.

clue.text: Broke open ribs, gutted in bar

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: but means except, as bar does in 'all bar one'

indicators.note: a gutted word has its insides removed, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: only its outer letters are used

explanation.surface: Someone's ribs were broken in a fight in a pub, leaving them gutted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub, but it means 'except'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that burst has split apart suddenly, which is to break open.

clue.text: Gully caught ball before you see one run

parts.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
O is round like a ball
U is text-speak for you
lo is an old word meaning look or see

explanation.surface: A cricket report: caught at gully off a ball before a single run.
explanation.walkthrough: Gully is a cricket fielding position, and the cricket words all around make it look like one; here it is a mountain ravine.
explanation.definitionFit: A couloir is a steep narrow gorge or ravine on a mountainside, a kind of gully.

clue.text: Ignoring backside in hour-glass shape possibly leaves wedge-like object?

indicators.note: the letters left could possibly be ordered another way, so they are rearranged
the backside word is ignored, taken out of the phrase

parts.note: taken as written
ass is the American word for backside

explanation.surface: A curvy figure with no bottom looks like a wedge.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by description: the blade of a plough is wedge-shaped.
explanation.definitionFit: The ploughshare is the pointed cutting blade of a plough, shaped like a wedge to turn the soil.

clue.text: Said bounder exercises right to have established character of Express?

indicators.note: the bounder's word is to be heard spoken, giving its sound

parts.note: a roo, a kangaroo, bounds along
PE is physical education
to bear is to have, as in bearing a name or a scar

explanation.surface: A cad is said to exercise his right to become an established figure at the Express newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounder' looks like an old word for a cad; it is a kangaroo. Rupert Bear has been a cartoon strip in Britain's Daily Express since 1920.
explanation.definitionFit: The checked-trousered cartoon bear has been a long-running fixture of the Daily Express newspaper.

clue.text: Credit for pollarding Japanese shrubs

indicators.note: pollarding cuts the top off a tree, so the first letter is removed

parts.note: kudos is credit or praise

explanation.surface: A gardener gets credit for pruning shrubs from Japan.
explanation.walkthrough: Udo is an East Asian plant grown for its edible shoots.
explanation.definitionFit: The udo is a Japanese plant of the ginseng family, cultivated as a vegetable.

clue.text: Left after a chap informally offers recess

indicators.note: the left letter comes after the word a

parts.note: taken as written
cove is old British slang for a chap or fellow

explanation.surface: A man casually offers time off, and someone departs afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcove is a recess set back into the wall of a room.

clue.text: Perhaps tracksuit garland found on certain river

parts.note: a lei is a Hawaiian flower garland
sure means certain
the Wear is a river in north-east England

explanation.surface: A tracksuit and a flower garland were found on the bank of a certain river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wear is a river in County Durham, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A tracksuit is an example of casual clothing worn for relaxing, as the 'Perhaps' signals.

clue.text: Changing hands, art house that's dreadful nevertheless

indicators.note: R and L stand for right and left hands, so one is swapped for the other

parts.note: its right-hand letter gives way to a left one
ugh is the exclamation for something dreadful

explanation.surface: A reviewer finds an arthouse film awful even after it changes ownership.
explanation.walkthrough: R and L are the usual crossword abbreviations for right and left, and 'hands' means sides here.
explanation.definitionFit: Although can mean 'but' or 'however', serving as a conjunction of concession like nevertheless.

clue.text: Isn't commonly opposed to shifting one

indicators.note: the letters shift about into a new order; the one letter moves along

parts.note: anti means opposed to

explanation.surface: A colloquial denial, against someone moving one thing.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the I moves: shifting 'one' (I) from the end to second place.
explanation.definitionFit: The colloquial contraction is a nonstandard everyday form of 'isn't' in speech.

clue.text: Evil lady goes topless subsequent to rants about sin

indicators.note: the lady piece comes after the rants piece
the word is turned about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: with the top cut off, the first letter goes

parts.note: an ogress is a female ogre

explanation.surface: A wicked woman strips off after ranting about sin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' paints a racy picture but means only that the first letter is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: To transgress is to break a moral law or commit a wrong, which is what to sin means.

clue.text: Old lizard's self-esteem stopping Truss bumbling round America

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the definition is the noun alone

indicators.note: the self-esteem word stops up a gap, sitting inside the rest
the jumbled letters go round the America letter
bumbling means clumsy and confused, so the name's letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
ego is one's sense of self-worth

explanation.surface: A political jibe: a fossil's self-regard halts Liz Truss blundering around the US.
explanation.walkthrough: Liz Truss was briefly UK Prime Minister in 2022. A stegosaur is a stegosaurus, the plated dinosaur.
explanation.definitionFit: The stegosaur was a plated dinosaur, an ancient reptile whose name means 'roof lizard'.

clue.text: Key drug in fruit engenders inactivity

indicators.note: the key and drug pieces go inside the fruit

parts.note: the quince is a hard yellow fruit
Esc is the escape key on a keyboard
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Putting a key drug into fruit leaves someone lethargic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key drug' reads as 'crucial drug', but the two words give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Quiescence is a state of rest or dormancy, the same as inactivity.

clue.text: Bishop & Son supports English missions

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting letter is underneath, so the rest sits above it

parts.note: RR, Right Reverend, is a bishop's title
the ampersand stands for 'and'
S is the genealogical abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A family firm, Bishop & Son, backs English missionary work.
explanation.walkthrough: The trade-name look of 'Bishop & Son' hides three separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Errands are short trips or tasks undertaken for someone, small missions.

clue.text: Pin catches narrow zip

indicators.note: the pin word catches and holds the other inside it

parts.note: a nog is a wooden peg or pin
thin means narrow

explanation.surface: A safety pin snags in a tight zip fastener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zip' looks like a fastener but means zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Zip is American slang for nothing at all, as in 'he won zip'.

clue.text: Maximum offence taken in speech

indicators.note: spoken aloud, the word sounds like the answer

parts.note: pique is resentment at a slight, offence taken

explanation.surface: Someone took the greatest possible offence at a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A peak is the highest point or level, the maximum reached.

clue.text: UK rock band identified with person's missing daughters

indicators.note: the daughters are missing, so both their letters go

parts.note: to place someone is to identify them, as in 'I can't place him'
bod is British slang for a person
D is the genealogical abbreviation for daughter; two daughters means two D's, one from each word

explanation.surface: A British rock group is linked to a man whose daughters have disappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: Daughters gives two D's, one from each word, both removed. Placebo are a British alternative rock band.
explanation.definitionFit: Placebo are a London alternative rock group formed in the 1990s, fronted by Brian Molko.

clue.text: Clapped-out, broken priest backsliding into fraud

indicators.note: the priest letters go into the fraud word, taking the place of its middle E

parts.note: deceit is fraud or trickery
Pr is the abbreviation for priest; reversed, it is broken apart around the E of the fraud word, which stays in the middle

explanation.surface: A worn-out, broken priest lapses into fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed priest letters do not go in as one block: they split to straddle the E of the fraud word.
explanation.definitionFit: Clapped-out is British slang for worn out and falling apart, just like something decrepit.

clue.text: Annalist's case for peace process you'll support initially

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the definition is the noun alone

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, its first and last letters

parts.note: only its outer letters are used

indicators.note: only the first letter of each word is taken

parts.note: the first letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A chronicler builds a case for a peace process that you will back from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Pepys kept the famous diary of 1660s London, including the Great Fire.
explanation.definitionFit: Pepys recorded the events of his day year by year, a chronicler or keeper of annals.

clue.text: Held forth split dictionary covers

indicators.note: the dictionary letters cover the other piece, around it

parts.note: OED is the Oxford English Dictionary
to rat or split on someone is to inform on them

explanation.surface: A speaker held forth about a dictionary whose covers had split.
explanation.definitionFit: Orated means spoke at length in a pompous way, which is what held forth means.

clue.text: Recognised landscape when escaping from trap

indicators.note: a trap is slang for the mouth, so words escaping from it are spoken aloud

parts.note: a scene is a view or landscape

explanation.surface: An animal gets away from a trap and dashes across a landscape, recognised by onlookers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trap' reads as a snare, but it is slang for mouth, as in 'shut your trap'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something seen has been noticed or acknowledged, the same as recognised.

clue.text: Busy magazine

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a detective, from the British slang 'busy' for a police detective
second meaning: the British satirical fortnightly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Busy' looks like an adjective, but it is old British slang for a detective; Private Eye is a long-running British satirical magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A private detective is a hired investigator, and the same phrase names the satirical news magazine.

clue.text: Still going up bottoms of best people? Absolutely

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters run from bottom to top
the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the last letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Elite people are still on the rise, absolutely.
explanation.definitionFit: Yet and still are adverbs meaning even now or up to this time.

clue.text: Amorous rendezvous in street succeeded following test

indicators.note: the street and succeeded letters follow on after the test word

parts.note: to try is to test
ST is the address abbreviation for street
S is the genealogical abbreviation for succeeded

explanation.surface: Lovers meet in a street once a test has been passed.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryst is a secret romantic meeting arranged between lovers.

clue.text: Execute banter, repulsed by curt cad

indicators.note: repulsed means pushed back, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to rag is to tease, banter with

indicators.note: curt means cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a rotter is a cad, a nasty man

explanation.surface: A curt, caddish man rebuffs teasing and threatens to kill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curt' reads as describing the cad's manner, but it cuts the word's tail off.
explanation.definitionFit: To garrotte is to kill by strangling with a cord or wire, a method of execution.
